hints: Start by reading the flat baseline at the left of each graph before the spike. What value does each trace sit at when at rest?
Now look at the top of each spike. Both reach the same peak, so think about how the size of the jump from baseline to peak will differ.
Compare the time axes carefully - Fig. 9.1 goes to 5 ms while Fig. 9.2 goes to 10 ms. How long does each spike last from start to return to baseline?
Look closely at what happens just after repolarisation in Fig. 9.1 around 3 ms. Does the same dip below baseline appear in Fig. 9.2?
walkthrough:
Compare the resting baselines**
Think of resting potential as the steady voltage when the membrane is at rest. In Fig. 9.1 the motor neurone sits at $-70 mV$, while in Fig. 9.2 the muscle fibre sits lower at $-90 mV$. So the motor neurone is less negative at rest.

Compare the size of the depolarisation**
Both traces peak at $+40 mV$, but because they start from different baselines the jump is different. For the neurone it is $+40 - (-70) = 110 mV$, for muscle it is $+40 - (-90) = 130 mV$. Always quote the calculated change with units to earn the comparison mark.

Compare the speed**
Look at the time scale. The neurone depolarises in about $1 ms$ and completes the whole action potential in about $2.7 ms$. The muscle takes about $2 ms$ to depolarise and about $4 ms$ overall. The neurone event is faster and shorter.

Spot the hyperpolarisation**
After repolarisation the neurone trace dips to about $-92 mV$ at 3 ms before returning to $-70 mV$. That overshoot is hyperpolarisation during the relative refractory period. The muscle trace in Fig. 9.2 returns straight to $-90 mV$ with no dip.

Final answer: Motor neurone has higher resting potential of $-70 mV$ vs $-90 mV$ in muscle; smaller depolarisation of $110 mV$ vs $130 mV$ in muscle; faster action potential of approx $2.7 ms$ vs $4 ms$ in muscle; hyperpolarisation occurs in motor neurone but not in muscle fibre.

hints: Fig. 9.3 shows tension stays flat for the first few ms after stimulation. What must spread into the fibre before anything mechanical can happen?
Think about which ion is stored inside the muscle fibre and released to act as the internal signal for contraction.
Link that ion to the regulatory proteins on the thin filament. What moves to uncover the sites where thick filament heads can attach?
walkthrough:
Spread of excitation takes time**
Stimulation triggers an action potential that spreads over the sarcolemma and down the transverse T-tubules into the centre of the fibre. That electrical spread plus the next chemical steps explain why tension does not rise immediately in the latent phase.

Calcium release is the coupling signal**
Depolarisation of the T-tubules causes the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release stored $Ca^{2+}$ by diffusion into the sarcoplasm surrounding the myofibrils. This is excitation-contraction coupling - electricity converted to a chemical signal.

Unblocking the thin filament to form cross-bridges**
$Ca^{2+}$ binds to troponin, which changes shape and pulls tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin heads can then bind to actin to form cross-bridges, ready for the contraction phase when tension will rise.

Final answer: T-tubules depolarised; $Ca^{2+}$ released from sarcoplasmic reticulum; $Ca^{2+}$ binds to troponin causing tropomyosin to move and expose myosin-binding sites on actin so myosin heads bind to form cross-bridges. No tension yet as this takes time.

hints: Relaxation needs many myosin heads to let go of actin. Do you think every sarcomere lets go at exactly the same instant?
walkthrough:
Relaxation is gradual because detachment is not synchronised**
When $Ca^{2+}$ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, tropomyosin re-covers the binding sites and myosin heads detach. Not all cross-bridges in all sarcomeres and fibres break at once, so force is lost progressively and the tension curve slopes down slowly over about 70 ms.
Final answer: Cross-bridges break / myosin heads detach from actin at different times in different fibres, so tension falls gradually.
